idiom_name: getter/setter pair over a nullable cache field
implementation_notes: The typed form of the JavaScript realization: a private cache field (null = dirty) is rebuilt by the getter, and every mutating method funnels through one invalidate() that empties the slot. TypeScript's types describe the cache's shape but cannot enforce its freshness - a readonly view or a mutated array bypasses the setter - so the invariant still needs a single choke point and the discipline to use it. Stage-3 decorators (available without experimentalDecorators since TypeScript 5.0) can wrap a getter/setter pair, but a decorator has no knowledge of which sibling property invalidates it, so the choke point normally stays ordinary class code. Where the derived value feeds UI, the typed form of a reactive primitive (Vue's computed<T>, MobX's @computed) is the framework-owned realization of the same idea.
pitfalls: Structural typing means consumers can build an object literal satisfying the interface without the class's invalidation paths; keep cached state in a class and expose a read-only view.
`??=` cannot distinguish a cached null from 'not computed' - use undefined or a separate boolean when null is a valid domain value.
TypeScript never checks that a mutation invalidated the cache; `readonly` only blocks assignments in typed code, and it is erased at runtime.
Definite-assignment assertions (`!`) on a cache field can hide the undefined state from the compiler while it is still observable at runtime during construction.

variants.name: Typed reactive computed value (framework-owned invalidation)
variants.idiom_name: Vue computed<T> / MobX @computed over observable state
variants.implementation_notes: Reactive libraries invert the responsibility: the primary data is made observable and the derived value is declared as a computed, which tracks its dependencies and re-evaluates only when one of them changed - the dirty flag, the invalidation edges and the recomputation timing all belong to the framework. In TypeScript the typed forms are first-class: computed<T> infers the getter's type, ref/reactive carry the primary state's type, and the unwrapping rules (.value in code, auto-unwrapping in templates) are checked. Use this when the derived value lives inside a reactive graph; hand-written flags remain the right tool for plain data structures, workers and libraries that must not depend on the framework.
pitfalls: Only tracked reads count as dependencies: reading plain module state (or Date.now()) inside a computed produces a value that never invalidates.
computed refs are read-only - assigning to one warns and does nothing, so invalidation must go through the primary state, never through the derived property.
Reactive wrappers are proxies around the object: passing the raw object around, or destructuring a ref out of the instance, silently loses reactivity.

The dependency graph is implicit at runtime: a computed that reads nothing observable recomputes on every access, and one that reads too much invalidates too often - re-check the dependency set when refactoring.
